sections.h2: What the York County Recorder of Deeds does
sections.html:
The Recorder of Deeds records and keeps every real estate document in York County, Pennsylvania. It also records military discharge papers and notary bonds and commissions. The recorder is an elected official serving a four-year term.

The office takes documents by mail, in person and through approved e-recording vendors. If your title company uses e-recording, the deed never has to be mailed. If you mail it, send a check or cash for the exact fee, because the counter does not take e-checks.

Indexing follows set rules. Every name variation on a document, such as a former name, a trading name or an also-known-as, is indexed, and the office may cross-index documents like affidavits and rights of way so each person or entity appears as both grantor and grantee. Where Mortgage Electronic Registration Systems acts as nominee for a lender, only that name is indexed, not the lender behind it. Expect those conventions when a title searcher reads your chain of title.

The Records Alert program tells a homeowner when any document is recorded against their property. It is worth signing up for if you own a house you are not living in.

Recording a deed runs $86.25, the same as a mortgage or quitclaim deed. That sum covers four pages and four names. Beyond that, each extra page is $2 and each extra name is $0.50. A separate $20 is charged for every parcel identification number the document mentions, a rule in place since January 1, 2025.

The Access to Justice fee is $41.25. Use the county's fee calculator (choose York) or the printable worksheet rather than adding figures from memory.

The counter takes cash, business checks and personal checks, and money orders payable to the Recorder of Deeds. A bounced check incurs a $50 charge. A surplus below $10 is kept, but a check exceeding the fee by more than $10 is returned for correction.

sections.h2: What a York County deed must contain
sections.html:
These are the points that most often cause a rejected deed. Check each before the closing agent sends it in:

  • The document must concern real estate, carry original signatures, and be properly notarized, in English or with an English translation.
  • A Uniform Parcel Identifier must appear on the document, with the property location (not a street address) beneath it at the top left. The county assessment office at 717-771-3253 or 717-771-4656 can supply it.
  • The grantor's name has to match the name on the prior deed exactly, so John Allen Smith cannot become John A. Smith.
  • The deed needs a precise address, because the assessment office uses it to mail tax bills.
  • The municipality, whether township, borough or city, belongs above the legal description.
  • The date on the deed must be the same as or earlier than the acknowledgment date.

When land lies in several municipalities, the deed must state the percentage split for local transfer tax. A family transfer where no tax is paid should say so in a typed statement on the deed. The Common Level Ratio factor is chosen by the date the document was signed and notarized, and the recorder's office at 717-771-9608 can supply factors for earlier years.

The state's own levy is 1 percent of the value of the real estate conveyed. Recorders bring it in along with any local transfer tax and pass the Commonwealth's share along.

A local portion rides on top. It varies with the borough or township and the school district, which is why a deed has to name each municipality. Get the exact local percentage for your parcel from the recorder or the closing agent before you estimate what you will net. The state holds buyer and seller jointly liable, while the sales contract decides who actually pays.

Exempt transfers include some among relatives, those to government bodies, burial-site deeds and property that passes by will or intestacy. Whenever the price paid is below full market value, a Statement of Value must accompany the deed, and an easement needs one too unless it belongs to a public utility.

Documents recorded in York County are public records, except military discharges. You can search free on the public computers in the Recorder's office during open hours, and printing costs $0.50 a page. Certified copies add $1.50 per document.

To search from home you need the deed book and page. Look up the owner's name in the county's real estate assessment database and the record book and page appear under the owner record. Documents can then be retrieved online through the Landex public records link on the county site. For anything recorded before 1944, researchers use the IQS site, where searching as a guest is free and printing is $0.80 a page.

sections.h2: York County housing at a glance
sections.html: York County stretches along the Susquehanna River to the Mason-Dixon line and has about 473,197 residents and 193,394 housing units. Owners live in 76.3 percent of occupied homes, and the median owner-occupied value is $248,600. Median household income is $84,829 and median gross rent is $1,193. Anyone selling an inherited house should also read up on Pennsylvania inheritance tax before listing.

sections.h2: Steps from closing to recorded deed
sections.html:
Your title company prepares the deed, checks it against the list above, and decides whether to e-record or mail it. Before it goes in, make sure the Uniform Parcel Identifier is on it, the grantor's name matches the prior deed, and every parcel number is counted for the $20 charge. Ask for the final total from the fee calculator so the check is exact.

A cash sale skips the lender's documents, but the recorder asks for the same things and charges the same fees. When the deed is recorded, the buyer's name enters the public record, and anyone searching the county's records can find it. Keep the recorded copy with your closing papers, and call the recorder's office if the deed does not show up in a search soon after closing.

faqs.a: Yes. York County takes recordings by mail, in person and through e-recording partners approved by the county. The counter does not accept e-checks, so fees paid in the office must be by cash, check or money order.

faqs.q: What does the York County recorder charge to file a deed?
faqs.a: The base fee is $86.25 for a deed, mortgage or quitclaim deed. It covers four pages and four names, and each parcel number on the document adds $20. Use the county's fee calculator to include every add-on.

faqs.q: Do I need a parcel identifier to record a deed in York County?
faqs.a: Yes. A Uniform Parcel Identifier is required on all documents before they are recorded. The assessment office can provide it. The property's location, not just its mailing address, goes beneath the UPI at the top of the deed.

faqs.q: Can I get an alert when a document is recorded against my York County property?
faqs.a: Yes. The Records Alert service tells a homeowner when any document is recorded against their property.

faqs.q: Is there a free way to look up a York County deed?
faqs.a: Yes. Public computers in the Recorder's office offer free searching during open hours, with $0.50 per printed page. Remote access runs through the county's Landex link, and the IQS site covers records before 1944 at $0.80 a page.
